short: Australia has no AI act. The Privacy Act 1988 binds, with an automated-decision transparency duty from 10 December 2026; the government established an Office of AI on 15 July 2026 and intends to legislate AI standards in early 2027.
title: Australia AI Laws
subtitle: No AI act yet: the Privacy Act binds, and AI standards legislation is due in early 2027
body_html:
Status at a glance

No AI act yet; privacy law binds. The government decided it "will not proceed at this time with previous proposals to introduce mandatory guardrails for AI development and deployment". On 15 July 2026 the Prime Minister announced: "Effective today, I am establishing The Office of AI in my own Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet." The National Cabinet communiqué of 26 August 2026 says "the Commonwealth intends to legislate the AI standards in early 2027", and speaks of "consistent mandatory standards for data centre energy, water and land-use". Until that legislation passes, the binding layer is the Privacy Act 1988, which gains an automated-decision transparency duty on 10 December 2026. Verified on 25 October 2026 against the Prime Minister's site, the Department of Industry's consultation hub and the OAIC.

Key instruments

InstrumentNumberPublishedIn force
Privacy Act 1988C2004A03712In force; APP 1.7 to 1.9 from 10 December 2026 (Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024)
Office of AI, Department of the Prime Minister and CabinetAnnouncement15 July 2026Established that day
Australian standards for AILegislation intendedNational Cabinet, 26 August 2026Early 2027, intended

Who regulates and enforces

  • Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC): enforces the Privacy Act, through civil penalty proceedings in the Federal Court.
  • Office of AI, Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet: coordinates the design of the AI standards.

Scope and reach

APP 1.7 covers an APP entity that arranges for a computer program to make, or do something substantially and directly related to making, a decision that could reasonably be expected to significantly affect an individual's rights or interests, using personal information. The Act's extraterritorial provision was not re-read.

Core obligations

  • From 10 December 2026: a privacy policy must describe the kinds of personal information used, and the kinds of decisions made, by computer programs (APP 1.7 to 1.9).
  • The rest of the Australian Privacy Principles, and sector rules.

Penalties

BreachMaximumProvisionEnforcer
Serious interference with privacy, by a body corporateThe greater of AUD 50,000,000; three times the value of any benefit the court determines; or, where the benefit cannot be determined, 30% of adjusted turnover in the breach turnover periodPrivacy Act s. 13G, as the OAIC guide states itFederal Court, on the OAIC's application
The same, by an individualAUD 2,500,000Privacy Act s. 13GFederal Court

What is coming next

  • 10 December 2026: the automated-decision transparency duty (APP 1.7 to 1.9) begins.
  • Early 2027: the Commonwealth intends to legislate the AI standards.

From voluntary guidance to legislated standards

Until July 2026 the Australian position was deliberately voluntary. The AI Ethics Principles of 2019 set eight principles; the Voluntary AI Safety Standard of September 2024 set ten guardrails; and the National AI Centre's Guidance for AI Adoption of October 2025, with its six essential practices (the AI6), replaced the safety standard as the government's primary reference for responsible AI. The National AI Plan published on 2 December 2025 kept that line, naming three priorities for 2026 (AI infrastructure, economy-wide adoption and skills, proportionate risk management) and preferring targeted amendments to existing law over a single AI statute; a Senate inquiry report (No. 111) on AI regulation had been tabled on 19 December 2025. The 15 July 2026 announcement reversed the method, not the goals: Australian Standards for AI are to be legislated in a single national framework, coordinated by the new Office of AI, with the first subjects named as mandatory standards for large AI data centres (location, energy, grid contribution, water), copyright protections for Australian creators, and AI consumer safety requirements set out on 20 July 2026. No exposure draft had been published when this page was checked, so the standards' coverage, regulator and penalties are unknown.

The binding date that is already law is 10 December 2026. On that day the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 brings new Australian Privacy Principles 1.7 to 1.9 into force: an APP entity that uses a computer program, AI included, to make or substantially assist a decision that could significantly affect a person's rights or interests must say so in its APP 1 privacy policy, describing the kinds of personal information used and the kinds of decisions made. The OAIC released an issues paper on 18 May 2026 and targeted guidance by September 2026; whether that guidance has been published was not checked. The same Act created the statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy, in force since 10 June 2025, and requires a Children's Online Privacy Code to be registered by 10 December 2026, with its commencement to follow. Deepfakes are already criminal: the Criminal Code amendments of 2024 criminalise transmitting non-consensual sexual deepfakes, and the government has said it will legislate against creation tools such as nudify apps.

The practical reading: existing law (Privacy Act, Australian Consumer Law, Copyright Act, Online Safety Act) applies now; the 10 December 2026 disclosure duty is the first AI-specific statutory date; the 2027 standards are real but incomplete, and their first wave looks like infrastructure and copyright rather than an EU-style risk regime.

The National AI Plan date (2 December 2025), the Guidance for AI Adoption (October 2025), the 20 July 2026 consumer safety priorities, the APP 1.7 to 1.9 numbering and the OAIC issues paper are as law-firm guides report them, not read on industry.gov.au or oaic.gov.au, which timed out, and are reported rather than verified. Not checked: whether the OAIC guidance on automated decision-making has been published.
